exact_claim: 6 June 1822, Mackinac Island: St. Martin, about 18, a voyageur (canoe-man) for the American Fur Company, is accidentally shot
notes: He was a voyageur, not a 'fur trader'

exact_claim: A musket loaded with powder and duck shot, fired from not more than one yard (less than a meter) away, into his left side
Beaumont reached him 25-30 minutes later; parts of the lung and the stomach protruded through the wound
notes: Narrate with restraint ('could see into his stomach'); never show it graphically

exact_claim: For 17 days everything he swallowed came back out through the wound
Beaumont tried for 8-10 months to close the opening; the only remaining option was stitching, 'an operation to which the patient would not submit'
notes: Becker Library (S2) notes modern speculation that Beaumont preferred it open - present as speculation only

exact_claim: A fold of stomach lining formed a natural valve/lid over the hole (winter 1823-24)
He lived with the opening for 58 more years (died 24 June 1880)
Experiment 1, 1 Aug 1825: six foods on a silk string inserted at noon
notes: High-seasoned a la mode beef, raw salted fat pork, raw salted lean beef, boiled salted beef, stale bread, raw sliced cabbage

exact_claim: At 1 pm the cabbage and bread were about half digested; at 2 pm cabbage, bread, pork and boiled beef were 'cleanly digested, and gone from the string'
notes: Beaumont later notes the bread may have fallen off when softened

exact_claim: When St. Martin felt ill, Beaumont dropped calomel pills directly into the stomach through the opening
238 numbered experiments (four series: 4+56+116+62)
Theories at the time included trituration (grinding) and putrefaction (rotting)
Beaumont reported applying his tongue to the stomach lining: no acid taste when empty, acid taste once food was present
notes: 'Beaumont wrote that he put his tongue to...' - his own report

exact_claim: Gastric juice: clear, a little salty, 'very perceptibly acid'; dissolved meat in vials outside the body when kept warm
notes: Modern framing: the stomach both churns and digests chemically

exact_claim: Beaumont recorded the subject's 'anger and impatience' and thought strong emotion disturbed digestion
In Aug 1825 St. Martin returned to Canada 'without obtaining my consent'
In Canada 4 years: married, two children, HBC voyageur 1827-28; Aug 1829 brought back ~2,000 miles with wife and children by fur-company agents 'at great expense to me'
1829-31 he worked as a servant between experiments - chopping wood, carrying loads
1831: the family paddled home in an open canoe via the Mississippi, Ohio, the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence to Montreal
Oct 1833 contract: one year as Beaumont's 'covenant servant', must submit to experiments 'on or in the stomach'; board, lodging and $150 a year (Nov 1833: 2 years, $400)
notes: Enrolled as Sergeant in a War Department detachment of orderlies

exact_claim: He could not read or write; his letters were written for him and signed with his mark
notes: Don't claim he signed the contract with an X - not established

exact_claim: June 1834: his wife was unwilling to let him go; he never worked for Beaumont again
1836-1852 letters and offers; 1846 Beaumont's son Israel sent to fetch him (Alexis owned a farm near Berthier); 1851-52 offer of $500 a year
Beaumont's last letter (15 Oct 1852): 'Don't disappoint me more nor forfeit the bounties and blessings reserved for you.'
1880: Osler wrote offering to pay for the stomach for the Army Medical Museum; refused
The family kept the body at home in hot weather to let it decompose and had the grave dug eight feet deep
primary_source: Osler 1902 quoting Judge Baby relaying Cure Chicoine
notes: Say 'According to the parish priest's account...'. No 'rot' wording

exact_claim: Comrades called him 'the man with a lid on his stomach'; at times he exhibited the wound to doctors and students; studied again in Philadelphia 1856
His age at death
notes: Sources give ages that are mutually inconsistent - don't state an age at death

exact_claim: Beaumont planned to take him to Paris/Europe; London society reportedly raised GBP 300-400 to bring him over (1840)
Beaumont died 25 Apr 1853 in St. Louis after a fall
